title: Corn Maze Shortcut
story: A farm cuts a maze into its corn field every autumn. The map is rows of characters: # is corn you cannot walk through, . is a path, S is the entrance and E the exit. Visitors move one square at a time, up, down, left or right.
The owner prints the fastest route's length on the ticket for visitors to beat. Some years a careless cut seals off the exit, and the ticket should say so.
task: Write shortestWalk(maze). maze is a list of equal-length strings. Return the smallest number of steps to get from S to E, where each step moves to a neighboring square up, down, left or right that is not #.
Return -1 if there is no way to reach E. You cannot step outside the map.
constraints: There is exactly one 'S' and exactly one 'E'

examples.explanation: The wall in column 2 blocks the top two rows. One fastest route: down to (1,0), right to (1,1), down to (2,1), right to (2,2) and (2,3), up to E at (1,3). 6 steps; nothing shorter gets around the wall.
The only square between S and E is corn and there is nowhere else to go, so the answer is -1.

hints: Take a pencil and the first example. Write 0 on S, 1 on every square one step away, then 2 on every new square next to a 1. What do you notice when you reach E?
The numbers spread in rings, like ripples. A square gets its smallest step count the first time a ring touches it and never needs another.
Which data structure lets you finish all the squares at distance 1 before starting any at distance 2? A stack does not do that, but another structure does.

Run a breadth-first search from S with a queue. Store each square's step count when you first add it, and mark it visited then. Skip walls, squares off the map and visited squares. The first time you take E out of (or put E into) the queue, its count is the answer. If the queue empties first, return -1.
bruteForce: Try every route with a depth-first search: walk from S, try each direction, back up at dead ends, and keep the shortest route to E. (The first route depth-first search finds is often a long winding one.)

On an open 20 × 20 field that is hopeless. There are only 400 squares, but there is an astronomical number of simple paths, and most of them walk through squares that could have been reached faster another way.

js: * @return {number} fewest steps from S to E, or -1

tests.note: exit right next to the entrance
must walk away from the exit first
spiral: the exit is deep inside
a depth-first search that goes down first finds a 6-step route; the answer is 2

js: for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
if (nr < 0 || nr >= rows || nc < 0 || nc >= cols) continue;
dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1; // first visit is the shortest
return -1; // queue ran out before reaching E
py: if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols and maze[nr][nc] != '#' and dist[nr][nc] == -1:
dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1  # first visit is the shortest
return -1  # queue ran out before reaching E
walkthrough: When every step costs the same, breadth-first search finds shortest routes for free. It handles all squares at distance 1, then 2, and so on, so it first reaches each square along a shortest route.
Trace the first example. The map is S.#. / ..#E / #... / ...., with S at (0,0) and E at (1,3).
• At distance 0 there is only S at (0,0).
• At distance 1 are (1,0) and (0,1). Their other neighbors are walls, the map edge, or each other.
• At distance 2 is (1,1). The square below (1,0) is #.
• At distance 6 is (1,3), which is E, reached from (2,3), so the function returns 6.
Mark a square visited when you add it to the queue, not when you take it out. Otherwise several neighbors can add the same square, wasting work and, on open fields, blowing up the queue.
solution.timeWhy: Each open square enters the queue at most once and checks four neighbors.
solution.spaceWhy: The distance grid and the queue each hold at most one entry per square.
solution.takeaway: For the fewest steps when every step costs the same, use breadth-first search. It explores in rings of equal distance, so it first reaches the target along a shortest route.
